title: Ordinal Arithmetic and the First Uncountable Ordinal

items.title: Transfinite recursion along the ordinals: a class rule determines exactly one operation defined at every ordinal
Ordinal addition exists and is unique: the clauses at $0$, at a successor and at a limit determine one operation, and its values are ordinals
Ordinal addition $\alpha + \beta$
Ordinal multiplication exists and is unique, and its values are ordinals
Ordinal multiplication $\alpha \cdot \beta$
Ordinal exponentiation exists and is unique, with the limit clause taken over $0 < \beta < \lambda$ so that $0^{\lambda} = 0$
Ordinal exponentiation $\alpha^{\beta}$, with the conventions $\alpha^{0} = 1$ and $0^{0} = 1$
$\alpha + \beta$ is the order type of $\alpha$ followed by $\beta$
$\alpha \cdot \beta$ is the order type of $\alpha \times \beta$ ordered by last differences, that is $\beta$ copies of $\alpha$
Monotonicity of ordinal $+$ and $\cdot$: strictly increasing and continuous in the right argument, weakly increasing in the left, with left cancellation
Ordinal addition is associative
Ordinal multiplication is associative, and $\alpha \cdot (\beta + \gamma) = \alpha\cdot\beta + \alpha\cdot\gamma$
For $\alpha \le \beta$ there is exactly one ordinal $\gamma$ with $\alpha + \gamma = \beta$
For $\alpha > 0$ every ordinal $\beta$ is $\alpha \cdot \xi + \rho$ with $\rho < \alpha$, in exactly one way

$\alpha^{\beta+\gamma} = \alpha^{\beta}\cdot\alpha^{\gamma}$ and $(\alpha^{\beta})^{\gamma} = \alpha^{\beta\cdot\gamma}$; and for $\alpha > 1$ exponentiation is strictly increasing with $\beta \le \alpha^{\beta}$

Cantor normal form: every nonzero ordinal is $\omega^{\beta_1}\cdot c_1 + \cdots + \omega^{\beta_k}\cdot c_k$ with $\beta_1 > \cdots > \beta_k$ and each $c_i$ a nonzero natural number, in exactly one way

On $\omega$ the ordinal operations are the Peano operations: $\omega$ is closed under ordinal $+$, $\cdot$ and exponentiation, and for naturals $m, n$ the ordinal $m + n$ and $m \cdot n$ are the natural-number sum and product
The first uncountable ordinal $\omega_1 := \aleph(\omega)$
$\omega_1$ is uncountable, every ordinal below it is at most countable, it is a cardinal and a limit ordinal, and its existence is a theorem of ZF
Cofinal subset of an ordinal

Assuming countable choice: every at most countable subset of $\omega_1$ is bounded below $\omega_1$, so no at most countable subset of $\omega_1$ is cofinal in it, and a supremum of at most countably many at most countable ordinals is at most countable
FALSE: ordinal addition is commutative
FALSE: ordinal multiplication is commutative
FALSE: $(\beta + \gamma)\cdot\alpha = \beta\cdot\alpha + \gamma\cdot\alpha$ for all ordinals
FALSE: $\beta < \gamma$ implies $\beta + \alpha < \gamma + \alpha$
FALSE: the ordinal $2^{\omega}$ is uncountable
Ordinal $\alpha^{\beta}$ and cardinal $\kappa^{\lambda}$ are different operations that share one notation
Choice ledger for this page: $\omega_1$ exists in ZF, and the boundedness theorem does not

title: Ordinal Arithmetic and the First Uncountable Ordinal — Examples

items.title: $1 + \omega = \omega$ and $\omega + 1 > \omega$, computed both from the recursion and as order types
$2 \cdot \omega = \omega$ while $\omega \cdot 2 = \omega + \omega$, pictured as order types
$\omega + \omega$ is at most countable although it is not order isomorphic to $\omega$: order type and cardinality are different invariants
$\omega^{2}$, $\omega^{\omega}$, and $\varepsilon_0 = \sup\{\omega, \omega^{\omega}, \omega^{\omega^{\omega}}, \dots\}$ satisfying $\omega^{\varepsilon_0} = \varepsilon_0$
The Cantor normal form of $(\omega^{2} + \omega\cdot 3 + 5) \cdot \omega^{2}$, computed by the division algorithm
Solving $\omega + \gamma = \omega\cdot 2$ and dividing $\omega^{2} + \omega + 3$ by $\omega$
A strictly increasing $\omega$-sequence of countable ordinals has a countable supremum, which is a countable limit ordinal below $\omega_1$
Refuted: some at most countable subset of $\omega_1$ is cofinal in it
$T_0$ (Kolmogorov) and $T_1$ (Frechet) spaces
A space is $T_1$ if and only if every singleton is closed, if and only if every finite subset is closed, if and only if its topology contains the cofinite topology
Separated sets: $\overline{A} \cap B = A \cap \overline{B} = \varnothing$
$G_\delta$ and $F_\sigma$ subsets of a topological space, agreeing with the real-line notion
Regular spaces and $T_3$ spaces, with the source disagreement over whether regularity includes $T_1$ stated explicitly
A space is regular if and only if every point has a neighbourhood base of closed neighbourhoods, if and only if $x \in U$ open gives an open $V$ with $x \in V \subseteq \overline{V} \subseteq U$
Urysohn ($T_{2\frac{1}{2}}$) space: distinct points have neighbourhoods with disjoint closures
Every Urysohn space is Hausdorff, and every regular $T_1$ space is Urysohn
Zero sets and cozero sets of continuous real-valued functions
Completely regular spaces and Tychonoff ($T_{3\frac{1}{2}}$) spaces
Every completely regular space is regular, and every Tychonoff space is $T_3$
Normal spaces and $T_4$ spaces, with the source disagreement over whether normality includes $T_1$ stated explicitly
A space is normal if and only if every closed $A$ inside an open $U$ admits an open $V$ with $A \subseteq V \subseteq \overline{V} \subseteq U$
A normal $T_1$ space is regular, hence $T_3$, hence Urysohn, Hausdorff, $T_1$ and $T_0$
Completely normal ($T_5$) and perfectly normal ($T_6$) spaces
Every completely normal space is normal, and every perfectly normal space is normal
In a metric space any two separated sets have disjoint open neighbourhoods, so every metrizable space is completely normal
In a metric space every closed set is a zero set and a $G_\delta$, and the distance function separates a point from a closed set, so every metrizable space is Tychonoff and perfectly normal

The implications proved on this page: perfectly normal and completely normal each give normal; normal with $T_1$ gives $T_3$; completely regular gives regular; regular with $T_1$ gives Urysohn, hence Hausdorff, hence $T_1$, hence $T_0$; and metrizable gives every one of them
The order topology on an ordinal, with the half-open intervals $(\alpha, \beta]$ and the initial segments $[0, \beta]$ as a basis
Every ordinal with its order topology has a basis of clopen sets, and is $T_1$, Hausdorff and regular
The $K$-topology on $\mathbb{R}$, generated by the open intervals together with their complements of $K = \{1/(n+1) : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$, is $T_1$ and Hausdorff but not regular
FALSE: every $T_1$ space is Hausdorff
FALSE: every normal space is Hausdorff, so the $T_1$ hypothesis in $T_4$ is redundant
FALSE: every Hausdorff space is regular
FALSE: a space in which every sequence has at most one limit is Hausdorff
Conventions on this page, and the two implications of the classical chain that are not available at this point in the reading order

title: Separation Axioms: the Hierarchy: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Sierpinski space is $T_0$ and normal but neither $T_1$ nor regular: normality without $T_1$ implies nothing
The particular-point topology is $T_0$ and not $T_1$, and it is not regular once the set has at least three points
The cofinite topology on an infinite set is $T_1$ but neither Hausdorff nor regular nor normal
The cocountable topology on $\mathbb{R}$ is $T_1$, has unique sequential limits, and is not Hausdorff
A discrete space satisfies every axiom in the chain; an indiscrete space with two points is normal, completely normal and regular, and fails $T_0$
Every closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is the zero set of $x \mapsto d(x, A)$ and the intersection of the open sets $\{x : d(x,A) < 1/(n+1)\}$
$\omega + 1$ as a convergent sequence with its limit, and $[0, \omega_1)$ in which every sequence that converges is eventually inside a countable initial segment
Refuted: every Hausdorff space built from ordinal spaces is normal. The deleted Tychonoff plank $((\omega_1 + 1) \times (\omega + 1)) \setminus \{(\omega_1, \omega)\}$ is Hausdorff and not normal

title: Function Space Topologies and the Exponential Law

items.title: The topology of pointwise convergence on $Y^{X}$, which is the product topology, and its restriction to $C(X,Y)$
A sequence converges in the topology of pointwise convergence exactly when it converges at every point
Locally compact metric space: every point has a compact neighbourhood
In a locally compact metric space every point has arbitrarily small closed balls with compact closure, hence a neighbourhood base of compact sets

Tube lemma: if $K$ is a compact subset of a metric space $X$, $Z$ is a topological space and $N$ is open in $X \times Z$ with $K \times \{z_0\} \subseteq N$, then $K \times W \subseteq N$ for some open $W \ni z_0$
The compact-open topology on $C(X,Y)$ for a metric domain $X$, with subbasis $S(K,V) = \{f : f[K] \subseteq V\}$
For a nonempty set $X$ and a metric space $(Y,d)$ the uniform metric $\bar\rho(f,g) = \sup_{x} \min\{d(f(x),g(x)), 1\}$ is a metric on $Y^{X}$
The topology of uniform convergence: the metric topology of the uniform metric on $Y^{X}$ and on $C(X,Y)$
Convergence in the uniform metric is exactly uniform convergence: one $N$ serving every point
The topology of compact convergence on $C(X,Y)$ for metric $X$ and $Y$: uniform convergence on each compact subset of $X$
For a metric domain and a metric target the compact-open topology on $C(X,Y)$ is the topology of compact convergence
On $C(X,Y)$ with $X$ and $Y$ metric, uniform convergence is finer than compact convergence, which is finer than pointwise convergence
A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, so $C(X,Y)$ is closed in $Y^{X}$ under the uniform metric
If $(Y,d)$ is complete then $Y^{X}$ is complete in the uniform metric, and so is $C(X,Y)$
The evaluation map $e : C(X,Y) \times X \to Y$, $e(f,x) = f(x)$
If $X$ is a locally compact metric space then the evaluation map is continuous for the compact-open topology
If $f : X \times Z \to Y$ is continuous then its transpose $F : Z \to C(X,Y)$, $F(z)(x) = f(x,z)$, is continuous for the compact-open topology, with no hypothesis on $X$ beyond being metric
The exponential law: for a locally compact metric $X$ and any spaces $Z$ and $Y$, transposition is a bijection between $C(X \times Z, Y)$ and $C(Z, C(X,Y))$ with the compact-open topology
Equicontinuity at a point, uniform equicontinuity, and pointwise boundedness of a family of maps between metric spaces
Dini's theorem: on a compact metric space a pointwise monotone sequence of continuous real functions converging pointwise to a continuous limit converges uniformly
FALSE: a pointwise convergent sequence of continuous functions converges uniformly on every compact set
FALSE: the compact-open topology on $C(X,Y)$ is metrizable for every metric $X$ and $Y$
FALSE: the evaluation map on $C(X,Y)$ with the compact-open topology is continuous for every metric $X$
Standing hypotheses on this page: a metric domain, where the target must be metric, and why the compact-open topology is built from metric compactness

title: Function Space Topologies and the Exponential Law: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $C([0,1], \mathbb{R})$ is complete, and on it the uniform metric and the supremum metric induce the same topology
The moving spikes on $[0,1]$ converge pointwise to $0$, do not converge uniformly, and do not converge in the topology of compact convergence
Refuted: convergence uniformly on every compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$ implies uniform convergence. The maps $x \mapsto x/(n+1)$ separate the two

On $C(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R})$ the compact-open topology has the sets $\{g : \sup_{[-m,m]} |f-g| < \varepsilon\}$ as a neighbourhood base, and $\mathbb{R}$ is locally compact so evaluation is continuous
The $1$-Lipschitz maps of a metric space into $\mathbb{R}$ form a uniformly equicontinuous family, and the distance functions $x \mapsto d(x,A)$ all belong to it
Refuted: a pointwise bounded family of continuous functions is equicontinuous. The spikes are bounded by $1$ everywhere and are not equicontinuous at $0$
Refuted: $C(X,Y)$ is closed in the topology of pointwise convergence. The ramps on $[0,1]$ converge pointwise to a discontinuous limit
The map $(x,z) \mapsto x \cdot z$ on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ and its transpose $z \mapsto (x \mapsto x \cdot z)$ traced through the exponential law
Dini's theorem applied to an increasing sequence of piecewise linear approximations on $[0,1]$, and what fails when the limit is not continuous
